items.passage:
Read the conversation between a student and a lecturer.

Jane: Dr Prasert, sorry to bother you — do you have a moment?
Dr Prasert: Of course, Jane. What can I do for you?
Jane: I'm applying for a summer research programme in Singapore, and I was wondering (1) ______
Dr Prasert: I'd be glad to help, though I should be frank with you. You took my introductory course along with about two hundred other students, so I could really only comment on your exam results.
Jane: Oh, I see. (2) ______
Dr Prasert: Not at all — it's a perfectly reasonable request. But the selection committee will be looking for evidence of how you work on a project. Didn't you do your independent study with Dr Malee?
Jane: Yes, last semester. (3) ______
Dr Prasert: Then she's the obvious choice. If she's willing, I could add a short note supporting your application as well.
items.stem: Which choice best completes gap (1)?
choices: whether you remembered who I was.
whether you might be willing to write me a letter of recommendation.
if you could tell me how to get to Singapore.
why you haven't sent my letter of recommendation yet.

explanation.en: Dr Prasert's reply ('I'd be glad to help... I could really only comment on your exam results') shows she has asked for a reference politely: 'whether you might be willing to write me a letter of recommendation.' Asking why it has not been sent assumes he already agreed.
explanation.th: คำตอบของ ดร.ประเสริฐ ('I'd be glad to help... I could really only comment on your exam results') แสดงว่าเจนขอจดหมายรับรองอย่างสุภาพ: 'whether you might be willing to write me a letter of recommendation.' ส่วนการถามว่าทำไมยังไม่ส่งเป็นการถือว่าอาจารย์ตกลงแล้ว

Read the conversation from a meeting at a software company.

Somsak: So, are we all agreed that we launch the app on the 1st?
Nina: I'm not sure I'd go that far. (5) ______ The payment feature still failed about one in fifty test transactions last week.
Somsak: One in fifty isn't bad, surely?
Nina: For a game, maybe. (6) ______ If customers lose money, we won't get a second chance.
Somsak: Fair point. But marketing have already booked the advertising for the 1st, and moving it would cost us.
Nina: (7) ______ Could we launch on the 1st without the payment feature and add it in an update once it's stable?
Somsak: That might work. Let me run it past marketing and get back to you by Friday.
items.stem: Which choice best completes gap (5)?
choices: I completely agree with the date.
The app is ready exactly as it is.
In fact, let's launch even earlier.
I think we may be rushing things.

explanation.en: 'I'm not sure I'd go that far' is a polite disagreement, followed by evidence of a problem, so 'I think we may be rushing things.' fits. The other replies agree with or go beyond the launch plan.
explanation.th: 'I'm not sure I'd go that far' เป็นการไม่เห็นด้วยอย่างสุภาพ แล้วตามด้วยหลักฐานปัญหา จึงต้องเป็น 'I think we may be rushing things.' ตัวเลือกอื่นเห็นด้วยหรือเร่งกำหนดการยิ่งขึ้น

items.passage:
Read the conversation in an electronics shop.

Customer: Hi. I bought this laptop here five weeks ago, and the keyboard has stopped working.
Assistant: I'm sorry to hear that. Unfortunately, our return period is thirty days, so (9) ______. However, it's still under the manufacturer's warranty.
Customer: How long would a warranty repair take?
Assistant: Usually two to three weeks — it has to go to their service centre.
Customer: Three weeks? I'm a student, and my final project is due in ten days. (10) ______
Assistant: I understand. Let me have a word with my manager... Right — she says that as you're only a few days outside the period, we can make an exception and exchange it today.
Customer: (11) ______ I really appreciate it.
Assistant: No problem. I'll just need the receipt and the original box.
Customer: I've got the receipt on my phone, but I'm afraid the box went out with the recycling.
Assistant: Hmm, that's normally a requirement... but given the circumstances, I'll make a note on the form.
items.stem: Which choice best completes gap (9)?
choices: the manufacturer's warranty has also expired
I can give you a full refund straight away
I'm not able to offer you an exchange or a refund myself
you'll have to buy a new keyboard yourself

explanation.en: 'Unfortunately' and the thirty-day limit signal a refusal, and 'However, it's still under... warranty' offers another route, so 'I'm not able to offer you an exchange or a refund myself' fits. A refund contradicts 'Unfortunately', and the warranty has not expired.

items.passage:
Read the seminar discussion between a tutor, Dr Lim, and two students, Anan and Sophie.

Dr Lim: Right, let's start. The article argued that universities should replace letter grades with written feedback. Anan, you were sceptical?
Anan: I was. I can see the appeal, but grades serve a purpose outside the university. Employers and scholarship committees need some way of comparing hundreds of applicants. (13) ______
Sophie: But that's exactly the article's point, isn't it? Grades are convenient for employers, not necessarily useful for learning. The study it cites found that students who got only comments improved more on the next assignment than students who got comments plus a grade.
Anan: (14) ______ That was one study, at one school, with fourteen-year-olds. I'm not sure it tells us much about university students.
Dr Lim: That's a fair methodological point. Sophie, how would you respond?
Sophie: I'd say the mechanism is likely to be similar. When students see a grade, they look at the number and ignore the comments. (15) ______
Anan: Possibly. But getting rid of grades entirely seems like throwing the baby out with the bathwater. Why not keep grades but release them a week after the feedback, so that students have to read the comments first?
Dr Lim: Interesting — that has actually been tried in a few places. Sophie?
Sophie: (16) ______ It keeps the comparison that employers want while giving the feedback a chance to be read. I'd still want evidence that it works, though.
Dr Lim: Good. Notice how you've both moved from opposing positions to something more nuanced. For next week, I'd like you to find any evidence on delayed grading and assess how strong it is.
items.stem: Which choice best completes gap (13)?
choices: Feedback is always more useful than grades.
Employers never look at grades anyway.
That's why I think grades should be abolished.

Saffron & Smoke, Sukhumvit Soi 31 — ★★★☆☆ reviewed by Daniel K.

Saffron & Smoke arrives with the kind of publicity most restaurants can only dream of: a celebrity chef, a six-week waiting list and an interior apparently inspired by a 1920s railway carriage. Expectations, in other words, could hardly be higher — which may be part of the problem.

Let's start with what works. The grilled river prawns, finished over charcoal and brushed with a tamarind glaze, are superb: smoky, sweet and sour in perfect proportion. A green curry made with smoked duck sounds like a gimmick but turns out to be the most thoughtful dish on the menu, the smoke deepening rather than overwhelming the curry. Service is warm and well informed, without the rehearsed speeches that plague many upmarket places.

Elsewhere, ambition outruns execution. A "deconstructed" som tam arrives as five separate elements on a slate, which looks striking but misses the point of the dish: the pounding together of flavours. The rice, astonishingly for a restaurant charging 480 baht for a bowl of it, was slightly undercooked on both of my visits. And desserts feel like an afterthought; a coconut panna cotta was perfectly pleasant and entirely forgettable.

Then there is the price. Dinner for two with a modest bottle of wine came to just over 7,000 baht. That is not unreasonable for this part of the city, but at this level a meal should be faultless rather than merely interesting.

Saffron & Smoke is not a bad restaurant — at its best it is a very good one. But it is not yet the restaurant its reputation suggests. Go for the prawns and the duck curry; skip the theatre.

Thai coffee farmers head for the hills as the climate shifts

CHIANG RAI — Coffee farmers in northern Thailand are planting at ever higher altitudes as rising temperatures and erratic rainfall make traditional growing areas less suitable for arabica, the high-quality bean that commands premium prices, according to a report published yesterday.

The report, by a regional agricultural research institute, found that the average altitude of new arabica plantings in three northern provinces had risen by around 150 metres over the past decade. Farmers interviewed for the study described flowering at unexpected times, more frequent pest outbreaks and beans ripening unevenly — all problems associated with warmer conditions.

"Arabica is a fussy plant," said the report's lead author, Dr Sunee Kittisak. "It does best in a fairly narrow range of temperatures. When nights stop being cool, the quality of the bean suffers, and so does the price the farmer can get."

Moving uphill is not a simple solution. Much of the higher land is forested, and some lies within protected areas. Conservation groups have warned that unchecked expansion could destroy forest that helps to regulate water supplies for communities downstream. "We understand the pressure farmers are under," said a spokesperson for one group. "But clearing forest to adapt to climate change would only make the underlying problem worse."

The report suggests alternatives. Growing coffee under the shade of taller trees can lower temperatures around the plants by several degrees, while also protecting the soil and providing habitat for birds. Some farmers are experimenting with more heat-tolerant varieties, though these tend to produce beans with a less distinctive flavour.

For many, the choice is economic as much as environmental. Shade-grown coffee yields less per hectare, at least in the first years, and specialty buyers do not always pay enough extra to make up the difference. Dr Sunee called for government support during the transition. "If we want farmers to adapt in a way that protects the forest, we have to make sure they can afford to," she said.

The Ministry of Agriculture said it would study the report's recommendations.

explanation.en: The article reports farmers 'planting at ever higher altitudes' because of climate change and then discusses the risks to forests and possible alternatives.

items.passage:
Why repetition makes falsehoods believable

In the 1970s, psychologists asked volunteers to rate how true a series of statements seemed. Some of the statements were accurate, some were false, and some were repeated across several sessions. The finding was striking in its simplicity: statements people had seen before were rated as more likely to be true, regardless of whether they actually were. Researchers named this the illusory truth effect, and in the decades since, it has been reproduced in dozens of experiments.

The explanation appears to lie in how the brain uses ease as a signal. A statement we have encountered before is processed more fluently — it feels familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for accuracy. In everyday life this shortcut usually serves us well, since most of what we hear repeatedly is, in fact, true. The trouble is that the shortcut cannot tell the difference between a claim repeated because it is correct and one repeated because someone wants us to believe it.

Perhaps the most unsettling finding is that knowledge offers less protection than we might hope. In one series of studies, participants who could correctly answer a factual question when asked directly were still more likely to rate a repeated false version of the fact as true. Knowing the right answer, it seems, does not guarantee that we will use that knowledge when a familiar-sounding claim slips past our attention. The effect is weaker for obviously absurd statements, but even for those it does not disappear entirely.

This has obvious implications in an age of social media, where the same claim may appear in a person's feed dozens of times, shared by different accounts and phrased in slightly different ways. It also creates a dilemma for those trying to correct misinformation. Repeating a myth in order to debunk it risks increasing its familiarity, and some early research suggested that corrections could "backfire", leaving people more convinced of the myth than before.

More recent work has softened that conclusion. Large studies have generally failed to find a consistent backfire effect; corrections usually reduce belief in false claims, at least in the short term. But the way a correction is framed matters. Researchers recommend leading with the accurate information rather than the myth, mentioning the false claim only once and clearly labelling it as false, and explaining why it is wrong rather than simply asserting that it is. An alternative explanation that fills the gap left by the myth tends to be more effective than a bare denial.

There is also evidence that people can be encouraged to pause. Simply asking participants to consider whether a statement is accurate when they first read it — rather than later — appears to reduce the effect of later repetition. Small changes in platform design, such as prompts that ask users whether they have read an article before sharing it, may work on the same principle.

None of this makes us helpless. But it does suggest that the feeling of "I've heard that somewhere" deserves more suspicion than we usually give it. Familiarity is evidence that a claim has been repeated — not that it is true.

explanation.en: The article explains the illusory truth effect and then discusses its implications for social media and for correcting myths. The backfire idea is said to have been 'softened', and knowledge offers 'less protection than we might hope'.

items.passage:
When a language falls silent

Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that around 40 per cent are endangered, many with only a few hundred or a few dozen speakers. Some estimates suggest that, at current rates, half of the world's languages could cease to be spoken by the end of this century. Unlike the extinction of a species, the loss of a language rarely makes headlines. Yet each one represents a distinctive way of describing the world, built up over many generations.

Languages rarely die because their speakers disappear. Far more often, they are abandoned gradually, as a community shifts to a more widely spoken language that offers access to education, jobs and national life. The process typically takes about three generations. Grandparents speak the heritage language fluently; their children understand it but use the dominant language in most situations; the grandchildren may know only a handful of words. By the time anyone notices, the chain of transmission from parent to child has already been broken — and that chain, rather than the number of speakers, is the most reliable indicator of a language's health.

Why should this matter to anyone outside the communities concerned? One answer is scientific. Languages vary in ways that challenge assumptions about what human language must be like. Some have no words for left and right, describing positions instead by the points of the compass; others mark in their grammar whether the speaker witnessed an event personally or heard about it from someone else. Every undocumented language that disappears removes evidence that linguists, psychologists and anthropologists might have used to understand the human mind.

Languages also carry knowledge of a more practical kind. Communities that have lived in one place for centuries often have detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and weather patterns, and some of this knowledge has proved valuable to scientists. But it would be a mistake to justify languages only by their usefulness to outsiders. For many speakers, a heritage language is bound up with identity, memory and a sense of belonging — values that cannot be measured in terms of information.

Reversing language shift is difficult but not impossible. Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in religious and written contexts, was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries. More modest successes include "language nests", in which young children are cared for entirely in the heritage language by older fluent speakers, and programmes that pair learners with elders. Technology helps too, from recorded dictionaries to messaging apps with keyboards for minority scripts.

What these efforts have in common is that they depend on the communities themselves. Outsiders can record and describe a language, but they cannot make anyone speak it. Revitalisation succeeds when speakers — especially parents — come to see the language not as a relic of the past but as something worth passing on. Whether that happens depends less on linguists than on the economic and social conditions that led people to abandon the language in the first place.

Unlike the extinction of a species, the loss of a language rarely makes headlines. Yet each one represents a distinctive way of describing the world, built up over many generations.

Languages rarely die because their speakers disappear. Far more often, they are abandoned gradually, as a community shifts to a more widely spoken language that offers access to education, jobs and national life. The process typically takes about three generations. Grandparents speak the heritage language fluently; their children understand it but use the dominant language in most situations; the grandchildren may know only a handful of words. By the time anyone notices, the chain of transmission from parent to child has already been broken — and that chain, rather than the number of speakers, is the most reliable indicator of a language's health.

Why should this matter to anyone outside the communities concerned? One answer is scientific. Languages vary in ways that challenge assumptions about what human language must be like. Some have no words for left and right, describing positions instead by the points of the compass; others mark in their grammar whether the speaker witnessed an event personally or heard about it from someone else. Every undocumented language that disappears removes evidence that linguists, psychologists and anthropologists might have used to understand the human mind.

Languages also carry knowledge of a more practical kind. Communities that have lived in one place for centuries often have detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and weather patterns, and some of this knowledge has proved valuable to scientists. But it would be a mistake to justify languages only by their usefulness to outsiders. For many speakers, a heritage language is bound up with identity, memory and a sense of belonging — values that cannot be measured in terms of information.

Reversing language shift is difficult but not impossible. Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in religious and written contexts, was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries. More modest successes include "language nests", in which young children are cared for entirely in the heritage language by older fluent speakers, and programmes that pair learners with elders. Technology helps too, from recorded dictionaries to messaging apps with keyboards for minority scripts.

What these efforts have in common is that they depend on the communities themselves. Outsiders can record and describe a language, but they cannot make anyone speak it. Revitalisation succeeds when speakers — especially parents — come to see the language not as a relic of the past but as something worth passing on. Whether that happens depends less on linguists than on the economic and social conditions that led people to abandon the language in the first place.

They are pointless once a language has fewer than 100 speakers.

explanation.en: Success 'depends less on linguists than on the economic and social conditions that led people to abandon the language', so revival may fail unless those reasons are also addressed.

is often graded more harshly
is usually rewarded more generously

explanation.en: 'Than' requires a comparative, and the point is that the system punishes risk: 'is often graded more harshly'. 'Rewarded more generously' contradicts the problem, 'as much... than' is ungrammatical, and a superlative cannot be followed by 'than'.
explanation.th: 'than' ต้องใช้กับขั้นกว่า และประเด็นคือระบบลงโทษการเสี่ยง: 'is often graded more harshly' ส่วน 'rewarded more generously' ขัดกับปัญหา 'as much... than' ผิดไวยากรณ์ และขั้นสูงสุดใช้กับ 'than' ไม่ได้

We tend to celebrate success and hide failure, (11) ______. Yet in many fields, failure is not the opposite of progress but a necessary part of it. Engineers learn more from a bridge that collapses than from a hundred that stand; (12) ______. The problem is that our education systems are designed to minimise failure rather than learn from it. A student who takes a risk on an ambitious project and falls short (13) ______ than one who completes a safe, predictable task competently. It is hardly surprising, then, that many students learn to play it safe.
Teachers, however, never grade projects at all.
As a result, students take more and more risks.

explanation.en: If risk-taking is graded more harshly, the logical consequence is caution: 'It is hardly surprising, then, that many students learn to play it safe.' Taking more risks is the opposite consequence.

skill.en: Organising sentences into a logical paragraph
skill.th: การเรียงประโยคเป็นย่อหน้าอย่างมีลำดับ

topic.th: เรียงประโยค: ข้อโต้แย้งและข้อแย้งกลับ

items.passage:
[1] Yet the benefits are frequently smaller than they appear.
[2] Whether tourism helps a community therefore depends less on the number of visitors than on who controls the industry.
[3] Visitors bring money that may otherwise be hard to find, and they create jobs in transport, food and accommodation.
[4] Meanwhile, the costs, from rising land prices to pressure on water supplies, are borne mainly by residents.
[5] Tourism is often presented as an ideal way for remote communities to earn an income.
[6] Much of the money spent by tourists goes to foreign-owned hotels and tour operators rather than to local people.
items.stem: The sentences above are in jumbled order. Which order makes the most logical paragraph?

explanation.en: [5] – [3] – [1] – [6] – [4] – [2]: the common view comes first and is supported by the benefits; 'Yet' turns to the counter-argument; the leakage of money explains why benefits are smaller; 'Meanwhile' adds the costs; 'therefore' concludes.
explanation.th: [5] – [3] – [1] – [6] – [4] – [2]: เริ่มด้วยความเชื่อทั่วไปและประโยชน์ที่สนับสนุน 'Yet' เปลี่ยนเป็นข้อโต้แย้ง เงินที่รั่วไหลอธิบายว่าทำไมประโยชน์น้อยกว่าที่คิด 'Meanwhile' เพิ่มเรื่องต้นทุน และ 'therefore' สรุป

skill.en: Organising sentences into a logical paragraph
skill.th: การเรียงประโยคเป็นย่อหน้าอย่างมีลำดับ

topic.th: เรียงประโยค: คำอธิบายทางวิทยาศาสตร์

items.passage:
[1] As a result, blue light is redirected across the whole sky and reaches our eyes from every direction.
[2] Sunlight appears white, but it is in fact a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum.
[3] At sunset, by contrast, light must pass through so much atmosphere that most of the blue has been scattered away before it reaches us.
[4] Such molecules scatter shorter wavelengths, at the blue end of the spectrum, far more strongly than longer, red ones.
[5] When it enters the atmosphere, this light collides with gas molecules that are much smaller than its wavelength.
items.stem: The sentences above are in jumbled order. Which order makes the most logical paragraph?

explanation.en: [2] – [5] – [4] – [1] – [3]: sunlight is introduced; 'it... this light' continues the description; 'Such molecules' refers to the gas molecules; 'As a result' gives the effect; 'At sunset, by contrast' adds the contrasting case.
explanation.th: [2] – [5] – [4] – [1] – [3]: เริ่มจากแสงอาทิตย์ 'it... this light' อธิบายต่อ 'Such molecules' อ้างถึงโมเลกุลก๊าซ 'As a result' บอกผล และ 'At sunset, by contrast' เพิ่มกรณีที่ตรงข้าม

skill.en: Organising sentences into a logical paragraph
skill.th: การเรียงประโยคเป็นย่อหน้าอย่างมีลำดับ

topic.th: เรียงประโยค: พัฒนาการทางประวัติศาสตร์

items.passage:
[1] Some historians argue that this, in turn, helped to make possible the rapid spread of new scientific and religious ideas.
[2] Within a few decades, printing workshops had spread to cities across the continent.
[3] Before the mid-fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, a process that could take months for a single volume.
[4] The resulting fall in the price of books made them available to a far wider readership.
[5] Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, which used movable metal type, changed this dramatically.
items.stem: The sentences above are in jumbled order. Which order makes the most logical paragraph?

explanation.en: [3] – [5] – [2] – [4] – [1]: the situation before printing comes first; 'changed this' refers back to hand-copying; 'Within a few decades' shows printing spreading; 'The resulting fall in price' follows from that spread; 'this, in turn' gives the wider consequence.
explanation.th: [3] – [5] – [2] – [4] – [1]: เริ่มจากสภาพก่อนมีการพิมพ์ 'changed this' อ้างถึงการคัดลอกด้วยมือ 'Within a few decades' แสดงการแพร่หลาย 'The resulting fall in price' เป็นผลที่ตามมา และ 'this, in turn' ให้ผลกระทบในวงกว้าง

items.subject: eng

skill.en: Organising sentences into a logical paragraph
skill.th: การเรียงประโยคเป็นย่อหน้าอย่างมีลำดับ

topic.th: เรียงประโยค: รายงานการวิจัย

items.passage:
[1] The researchers suggest that lyrics compete with reading for the brain's language-processing resources.
[2] Participants were randomly assigned to complete a reading test in silence, with instrumental music or with songs containing lyrics.
[3] They caution, though, that the test lasted only 20 minutes and that longer tasks might produce different results.
[4] The group exposed to lyrics, however, scored on average 12 per cent lower.
[5] To investigate whether background music affects concentration, researchers recruited 90 university students.
[6] Those who worked in silence or with instrumental music achieved similar scores.
items.stem: The sentences above are in jumbled order. Which order makes the most logical paragraph?

explanation.en: [5] – [2] – [6] – [4] – [1] – [3]: the aim and participants come first, then the method; results follow ('similar scores', then 'however... lower'); the explanation of the lyrics result comes next; 'They caution, though' adds the limitation at the end.
explanation.th: [5] – [2] – [6] – [4] – [1] – [3]: เริ่มจากจุดประสงค์และผู้เข้าร่วม ตามด้วยวิธีการ ผลการวิจัย ('similar scores' แล้ว 'however... lower') คำอธิบายผลของเพลงที่มีเนื้อร้อง และ 'They caution, though' เป็นข้อจำกัดในตอนท้าย

topic.th: เรียงประโยค: การยอมรับและโต้แย้ง

items.passage:
[1] In the short term, this complaint is sometimes justified.
[2] This is the reverse of a well-documented pattern in which building more roads simply encourages more driving.
[3] Critics of new cycle lanes often argue that they cause traffic jams by taking space away from cars.
[4] Judging cycle lanes by their effect in the first few months may therefore be as misleading as judging a new road by its first week.
[5] Over time, however, well-connected networks tend to attract people who previously drove, reducing the number of cars on the road.
items.stem: The sentences above are in jumbled order. Which order makes the most logical paragraph?

explanation.en: [3] – [1] – [5] – [2] – [4]: the critics' claim comes first; 'this complaint' refers to it; 'Over time, however' contrasts with 'In the short term'; 'This is the reverse' comments on the long-term effect; 'therefore' concludes.
explanation.th: [3] – [1] – [5] – [2] – [4]: ข้อกล่าวอ้างของฝ่ายวิจารณ์มาก่อน 'this complaint' อ้างถึงข้อกล่าวอ้างนั้น 'Over time, however' ตรงข้ามกับ 'In the short term' 'This is the reverse' อธิบายผลระยะยาว และ 'therefore' สรุป
